text: The core market gap is the specific join between a merge-triggered repo interrogation, a structured product-context interview captured while the author still has context, and a demo spec as intermediate representation from which multiple formats are rendered.
No verified existing product connects a git merge event through a structured PM-style interview to a multi-format demo artifact as a single flow.
The demo script should be the intermediate representation (canonical artifact) from which screenshots, video, and voiceover are derived.
Automated headless UI capture is the highest-risk component due to authentication, seed data, non-deterministic UI state, and selector fragility.
A hybrid architecture is recommended: CI/repo event creates a draft and triggers the interview, while visual capture is a separate, deferrable, opt-in action.
The MVP should produce only demo scripts (not video or screenshots) to validate the core thesis before investing in capture automation.
Every interview question must be pre-filled with a best-effort draft answer derived from repo/PR facts; the engineer's role is to edit or confirm, not author from scratch.

Confidently wrong pre-filled answers (hallucinated customer segment, benefit, or outcome) are the highest-trust-destruction failure mode and should be avoided by preferring explicit uncertainty over confident wrongness.
The trigger should not fire on every merge; a gate based on a PR label, UI-file heuristic, or explicit opt-in is required to avoid interview fatigue and low-signal outputs.

Storybook combined with visual regression tools (e.g., Chromatic) represents an under-appreciated adjacency for screenshot capture because component stories are already rendered and screenshotted per commit.
The demo spec data model should carry provenance metadata (source and confidence) on every human-context field to distinguish inferred from human-confirmed values.

The strongest argument against building the product is that the underlying cause of missing demos may be a prioritization or culture problem rather than a friction problem, meaning the tool will be adopted only by teams already disciplined enough to make demos without it.
The interactive (editor/agent/CLI) architecture reintroduces the 'extra step that gets skipped' risk because it depends on the engineer remembering to invoke it after merge.

Downstream reuse of generated artifacts (scripts used in changelogs, sales enablement, or external communications) is the critical validation signal; generation without reuse indicates the problem statement is wrong.

Identifying the user-visible surface from a diff is a non-trivial classification problem; backend refactors, dependency bumps, and internal-tool changes will produce false positives without an explicit classifier or PR label.
Remotion (React-based programmatic video) is a strong fit for the video rendering layer because the intermediate representation is a structured script.

The product could potentially be built as a layer on top of existing interactive demo platforms (e.g., Supademo or Arcade) via their APIs rather than as a standalone product, which would weaken the standalone-product thesis if their APIs permit programmatic demo creation.
Danger.js is directly relevant scaffolding for the CI/PR-comment orchestration layer of this product.
The buying center for this product is unclear because it spans engineering, PM, marketing, support, and sales enablement, creating a horizontal-tool adoption problem.

A Phase 0 discovery step (user interviews and hand-classification of recent merged PRs) should precede any software build to validate that the pain is real and that a sufficient fraction of merges are demo-worthy.
The interview should address whether the feature is intended for the PR author or a designated demo-owner, as the RFC's assumption that the author is the right interviewee deserves explicit testing.
